newsitem.title: UK: Two-minded Swissie seen up on mark, down vs dlr.
newsitem.headline: Two-minded Swissie seen up on mark, down vs dlr.

text.p: The Swiss franc, which stormed into the forex spotlight this week, is set to tread a drastically different path to the mark and dollar, analysts say.

An unusually volatile franc caught many market players on the hop on Thursday when it touched an 11-month high against the mark of 80.85 centimes before slithering back down in tandem with the dollar's surge to a 47-month peak against the Swiss unit.
That dollar/Swiss strength should continue, but the mark's European monetary union woes can only mean the German currency weakens further against the Swiss, analysts said on Friday.
Until Thursday, "the Swissie was very, very strong. It was the only European currency against which the dollar had not made new highs," said Peter von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS here.

Dollar/Swiss' sudden upswing -- after lagging the broad rally which has taken the dollar to six-year highs against the mark -- squeezed a market which had found itself extremely short of mark/Swiss, traders said.
The dollar extended its rally on Friday to reach its highest level in almost four years of 1.5176 francs, as dollar/mark tested fresh highs above 1.84.
"The Swissie will be a European currency from now on -- it will depreciate as part of a European bloc against the dollar," said von Maydell.
The mark glanced a session peak of 82.62 Swiss centimes on Friday, well up from its previous European close of 82.01 and sharply higher than the 80.90 low hit during Thursday's trading.
But that rally is not expected to last.
"Mark/Swiss is on the way down still," said von Maydell.
Analysts said the dip in the franc had not come too soon.
"It was getting to very overvalued levels -- everyone's been waiting for the Swiss franc to weaken," said Michael Lewis, senior international economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell here.

That can only be bad news for the struggling Swiss economy, he said. "The economy is just so weak...the Swiss National Bank wants to create an environment for the economy to recover, and a strong currency isn't going to help."
However, the main boost to the Swiss franc has been something beyond the SNB's control -- European Economic and Monetary Union.

The growing conviction that the mark will bow out to a softer, more inflation-prone euro in 1999 has driven funds out of marks into perceived safe havens like the dollar, sterling, the Swedish crown and the Swiss franc.
But Swiss fundamentals ought to give pause for thought to investors seeking refuge, analysts warned.

"We see sterling and the dollar as better 'safe-haven' currencies than the Swiss franc in the 'broad-EMU/soft euro' scenario because of poorer Swiss fundamentals," said Claudio Demolli, foreign exchange analyst at Merrill Lynch.
Analysts said the franc's sharp decline against the dollar might ease SNB concerns about its strength against the mark.
The Swiss franc has lost 28 percent against the dollar in the last year. Against the mark, by contrast, it has appreciated more than eight percent since its rally began in February.
